nameStory: The Michigan lily gets its name from the state where it was first scientifically described and cataloged by botanists. While it's called the 'Michigan' lily, this beautiful wildflower actually grows across a much wider range, from the Great Lakes all the way down to Georgia and out to the Great Plains.
description: The Michigan lily is a stunning wildflower that can tower up to 5 feet tall, making it one of our more impressive native lilies. It produces showy orange flowers with dark brown spots and distinctively curved-back petals that seem to flip inside-out. This bulbous perennial emerges from underground each spring and puts on its spectacular flower show during summer months, creating bright splashes of orange in prairies and meadows.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Brilliant orange blooms with dark brown or black spots, featuring petals that curve sharply backward (recurved) almost touching behind the flower, creating a distinctive turban or cap shape

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged in circular clusters (whorls) around the stem at regular intervals, with a smooth texture and prominent parallel veins

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, sturdy single stem reaching 3-5 feet high, growing from an underground bulb and typically producing 1-3 flowers at the top

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Six prominent stamens with dark reddish-brown anthers that dangle conspicuously from the center, often dusting visitors with rusty-colored pollen

habitat: In New England, Michigan lily is extremely rare and found primarily in moist prairies, wet meadows, and prairie-like openings. It prefers sunny to partially shaded locations with rich, moist soils and good drainage. You're most likely to encounter it in restored prairie habitats or naturalized areas rather than deep forests.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from the bulb in late spring, with the distinctive whorled leaves unfurling as the stem grows rapidly upward.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs in mid to late summer, when the spectacular orange flowers open and attract butterflies and hummingbirds with their nectar.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules develop, while leaves begin to yellow and die back as the plant stores energy in its underground bulb.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no above-ground parts visible, surviving as a bulb buried several inches deep in the soil.

funFact: Michigan lilies are expert chemists - their bulbs were traditionally used by Native Americans as food after careful processing to remove bitter compounds, and a single bulb can live for decades underground, sometimes not flowering for years until conditions are just right.
confusionNotes: Michigan lily is easily confused with the more common Turk's-cap lily and the introduced tiger lily. The key difference is in the spots: Michigan lily has brown-black spots that are more scattered, while tiger lily has very dense black spots and fuzzy orange bumps (bulbils) along the stem. Turk's-cap lily is much taller (up to 8 feet) and has more flowers per plant.
contextualKnowledge: With only 3 recorded observations in New England, Michigan lily is essentially at the very eastern edge of its natural range here. Most of the Michigan lilies you might see in New England gardens are actually cultivated plants rather than wild natives, as this species is more at home in Midwestern prairies than New England forests.
compareHints: Among New England's true lilies, Michigan lily is distinguished by its moderate height (shorter than Turk's-cap lily but taller than wood lily) and its orange color with backward-curved petals. Unlike the upward-facing wood lily or the yellow Canada lily, Michigan lily's flowers nod downward with those dramatically reflexed petals. The whorled leaf arrangement helps separate it from many other orange wildflowers that aren't true lilies at all.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's true lilies, Canada lily is the only one with consistently downward-facing, bell-shaped flowers in yellow to orange shades.
Unlike its relatives Canada lily and Turk's-cap lily which have downward-facing or nodding flowers, wood lily is the only native lily in New England that consistently faces its flowers upward.
Among New England's lilies, tiger lily is the only one with black bulbils in the leaf joints and the only non-native species commonly encountered.

Among New England's native lilies, Turk's-cap lily is the tallest and most dramatic, with its hanging orange flowers and completely recurved petals setting it apart from the upward-facing Canada lily and the smaller, red Wood lily.
Unlike our native Canada lily and Turk's-cap lily which have drooping, downward-facing flowers, Formosa lily blooms face outward horizontally.
Unlike our native lilies, martagon lily has distinctly whorled leaves rather than alternate or scattered leaf arrangements.
